requirement.description:
24 total units are required with at least 20 units as upper-division from all courses listed below, and the Area A and Area B breadth requirements must be accounted for within those 24 total units
[Important Note: A single course can only apply to satisfying one of the distribution requirements even if it is listed under multiple areas, so a single course cannot be applied under any two distribution requirements.]

sections.notes: Substitutions and waivers are subject to approval by the Executive Director or the Faculty Chair of the Medieval Studies Program.

narrative: The Medieval Studies minor consists of at least 24 total units, at least 20 of which must be upper-division, with courses accounting for the breadth requirements listed below. Note that all courses completed towards the minor must be from courses outside of the student’s major department. All courses to be applied to the minor must be completed on a letter grade basis. The advisors for the minor are the Executive Director and the Faculty Chair of the Medieval Studies Program.

Students must consult the General Catalog for prerequisites to required courses.
The following conditions must also be met for official recognition of the minor:
- The sponsoring department reports completion of the minor prior to the posting of the degree.
- At least 18 upper-division quarter units are completed for the minor. (Waivers cannot reduce the requirement below this number.)
- The UC grade-point average in ALL applied upper-division courses is 2.0 or higher.
- No more than 4 upper-division units overlap between this minor and the upper-division portion of other minor(s). If overlap with other minor(s) is greater, only the first minor reported will be recognized.

nodes.title: Survey: Eccentric Images
groups: UPPER DIVISION: A-2) Art, Architecture or Music (image, sound, material objects)
nodes.description: This course examines the history of art through some of its strangest images, including spatial illusions, chance images, hidden faces and monsters, reversible images, caricatures and others. Primarily focused on the early modern period (1400-1750), we also consider similar experiments from other cultures.

nodes.title: Medieval Architecture: From Constantine to Charlemagne
groups: UPPER DIVISION: A-2) Art, Architecture or Music (image, sound, material objects)
nodes.description: A survey of the architecture in Italy, France, Spain, Germany, and England from the early Christian through the Carolingian periods.

nodes.title: The Global Middle Ages: Visual and Cultural Encounters in the Medieval Mediterranean
groups: UPPER DIVISION: A-2) Art, Architecture or Music (image, sound, material objects)
nodes.description: Focusing on the Mediterranean, this course considers visual manifestations of exchange. Its goal is to examine the complexity of religious, political, and visual interactions in the Middle Ages, a period that brought together diverse religious communities, generating both social frictions and new cultural forms. Students will study the dynamic interplay among Christian, Jewish, and Islamic visual cultures as they developed and coalesced through commerce, gift exchange, the reinterpretation of pre-existing forms, and the reuse of objects and spaces.

nodes.title: Introduction to Medieval Art and Architecture
groups: UPPER DIVISION: A-2) Art, Architecture or Music (image, sound, material objects)
nodes.description: This course explores the soaring cathedrals, monstrous sculptures, and marvelous images that inspired The Lord of the Rings and Game of Thrones. Beginning with the fourth-century rise of Christian images and ending with the advent of print, it traces how images developed new roles and reinvented old ones over the course of the Middle Ages. Investigating architecture, sculpture, and manuscripts in their historical contexts, it asks why medieval objects look the way the do and how viewers saw them.

nodes.title: Art and War
nodes.description: We often think about art as a bridge between cultures and look to masterpieces like the Sistine Chapel as the height of a nations cultural achievements. But during times of war, art can become military targets and destroyed, or used to create enemies. Conversely, art has been employed to resist political establishments, critique violence, and provide therapy for veterans. Drawing examples from different time periods, this course investigates the myriad ways art has been usedand abusedduring military conflict.

nodes.title: Painting in the 15th-Century Netherlands
groups: UPPER DIVISION: A-2) Art, Architecture or Music (image, sound, material objects)
nodes.description: Netherlandish painting from C1400- C1500 examined in its social, religious,and cultural contexts. Van Eyck, Rogier, Bouts and Memling, among others.

nodes.title: Painting in the 16th-Century Netherlands
groups: UPPER DIVISION: A-2) Art, Architecture or Music (image, sound, material objects)
nodes.description: Painting of the low countries from C1500-C1600, placed in its social and cultural contexts. Artists studied include Bosch and Bruegel. continuation from 107A, but may be taken separately.

nodes.title: Renaissance Kunst- and Wunderkammern: the First Museums
groups: UPPER DIVISION: A-2) Art, Architecture or Music (image, sound, material objects)
nodes.description: In the sixteenth century, wealthy merchants and powerful princes in Europe began assembling vast collections that aspired to contain all possible knowledge of all possible things. From these remarkably diverse collections called Kunst- and Wunderkammern (German), studioli (Italian), and curiosity cabinets (English)arose our modern museums of art, science, history and technology, as well as modern research collections in universities. This course explores these fascinating collections, the purposes that they served and the circumstances in which they were created.

groups: UPPER DIVISION: A-2) Art, Architecture or Music (image, sound, material objects)

nodes.title: Mediterranean Cities
groups: UPPER DIVISION: A-2) Art, Architecture or Music (image, sound, material objects)
nodes.description: An exploration of the most important Medieval cities of the Mediterranean world, their urban forms, layout, architecture, and physical patterns. Venice, Cairo, and Baghdad will be among the cities discussed.

nodes.title: Islamic Architecture 650-1400
groups: UPPER DIVISION: A-2) Art, Architecture or Music (image, sound, material objects)
nodes.description: Islamic architecture between 650 and 1400 in its historical context.

groups: UPPER DIVISION: A-2) Art, Architecture or Music (image, sound, material objects)

nodes.title: Chinese Painting I
groups: UPPER DIVISION: A-2) Art, Architecture or Music (image, sound, material objects)
nodes.description: Chinese painting and theory, from beginnings through the fourteenth century. Introduction to major developments and masters in their cultural context with a focus on meaning and agency.

nodes.title: The Art of the Chinese Landscape
groups: UPPER DIVISION: A-2) Art, Architecture or Music (image, sound, material objects)
nodes.description: Chinese approaches to landscape as subject matter in art, with a focus on painting and garden architecture. The course begins with the immortality cult in the Han Dynasty (206 B.C.-A.D.221) and ends with contemporary artists of the twentieth century.

nodes.title: Seminar in Medieval Art
groups: UPPER DIVISION: A-2) Art, Architecture or Music (image, sound, material objects)
nodes.description: Advanced studies in Medieval art. Topics will vary. This course requires weekly readings and discussion, and the writing of a research seminar paper.

nodes.title: Seminar in Medieval Architecture & Sculpture
groups: UPPER DIVISION: A-2) Art, Architecture or Music (image, sound, material objects)
nodes.description: Advanced studies in Medieval architecture and sculpture. Topics will vary. This course requires weekly readings and discussion, and the writing of a research seminar paper.

groups: UPPER DIVISION: A-2) Art, Architecture or Music (image, sound, material objects)

nodes.title: Major Works in European Literature
groups: UPPER DIVISION: A-3) Literature or Written Culture (text, writing)
nodes.description: A survey of European literature. Classical and medieval literature from Homer to Dante.

nodes.title: Tales of Love in the Western Tradition
groups: UPPER DIVISION: A-3) Literature or Written Culture (text, writing)
nodes.description: A comparative and interdisciplinary approach to the literatures and philosophies of love, desire, and sexuality in the western world, in antiquity, the Middle Ages, and the Renaissance. In English.

nodes.title: Dante's Divine Comedy
groups: UPPER DIVISION: A-3) Literature or Written Culture (text, writing)
nodes.prereq_text: Upper division standing or instructor approval required
nodes.description: Dante's masterpiece, The Divine Comedy, remains among the most astonishing works of world literature. This course follows the pilgrim's progress through Inferno, Purgatorio and Paradiso in search of love that moves the sun and the other stars.

nodes.title: East Asian Buddhist Poetry
groups: UPPER DIVISION: A-3) Literature or Written Culture (text, writing)
nodes.description: Introduces Buddhist poetry of China, Japan, and Korea. Emphasizes the diversity of literary encounters with the teachings and practices of Buddhism. Topics include Hanshan, Basho, Zen koans, Gary Snyder, and monastery cats.

nodes.title: Nature and Ethics in Chinese Philosophy
groups: UPPER DIVISION: A-4) Religion, Philosophy or Science
nodes.description: A look at how major thinkers in classical Chinese thought grappled with questions related to the individual's place in society and their relationship to their environment. Highlighting their relevance, classical views will be applied to contemporary ethical, social, and environmental debates.

nodes.title: Masterpieces in Chinese Literature
groups: UPPER DIVISION: A-3) Literature or Written Culture (text, writing)
nodes.description: Examines a selection of works from Chinese literature, with the goal of understanding the major genres and their development over time. The cultural roles of literature, as well as criteria for critical evaluation, are also addressed.

groups: UPPER DIVISION: A-4) Religion, Philosophy or Science

nodes.title: Tang Literary History
groups: UPPER DIVISION: A-3) Literature or Written Culture (text, writing)
nodes.description: Examines the history of literature during the celebrated Tang dynasty (618907). Focus on changes in literary norms, practices, and theory as they intersected with societal, political, intellectual, and religious developments. Also considers problems of historiography. Emphasis varies by quarter.

nodes.title: Storytelling and Chinese Culture
groups: UPPER DIVISION: A-4) Religion, Philosophy or Science
nodes.prereq_text: Reading knowledge and skills in advanced modern Chinese
nodes.description: Taught in Chinese, this course is designed to elucidate Chinese history and culture from the perspective of storytelling. Readings are original narrative texts from the Tang, Song, and Ming-Qing eras.

groups: UPPER DIVISION: A-4) Religion, Philosophy or Science

nodes.title: Ancient Magic and Modern Revivals
groups: UPPER DIVISION: A-4) Religion, Philosophy or Science
nodes.description: Explores the practice of magic in classical antiquity, beginning with the archaic period and ending in the seventh century CE. This historicized survey of practices, laws, and literary representations serves as a springboard for reflecting on magic as a social phenomenon and category of thought, and for discussion of the modern reception and contemporary revivals of Greco-Roman magic.

nodes.title: The Fall of the Ancient Republic: Cicero, Caesar, and Rome
nodes.description: The tumultuous end of the Roman Republic, from Tiberius Gracchus (133 BC) to the Rubicon (49 BC), had profound importance for the history of the West and produced a fascinating literature of crisis in the writings of Sallust, Cicero, Catullus, and Caesar.

groups: UPPER DIVISION: A-3) Literature or Written Culture (text, writing)

nodes.title: Chinese Civilization
nodes.description: A survey of the history of Chinese civilization from 2,000 BCE to the present, focusing on the origins and later development of political, social, economic, philosophical, religious, and cultural traditions.

nodes.title: Christianity, Judaism, and Islam in China
nodes.description: Examines Christian, Jewish, and Muslim communities in the Middle Kingdom from 500 to the present day, debunking the myth of a closed and insular China.

nodes.title: Introduction to Literary Study
nodes.description: Acquaints students with purposes and tools of literary interpretation. Introduces techniques and vocabulary of analytic discussion and critical writing. Some emphasis on poetry with attention also to drama, essay, and the novel.

nodes.title: Introduction to Old English Language and Literature
groups: UPPER DIVISION: A-3) Literature or Written Culture (text, writing)
nodes.prereq_text: Writing 2 or 50 or 109 or English 10; upper-division standing.
nodes.description: Introduction to Old English language and literature. Students learn to read and translate a selection of prose and verse works. A full description for any given quarter will be available on the English Departments website.

nodes.title: Old English Literature: Beowulf
groups: UPPER DIVISION: A-3) Literature or Written Culture (text, writing)
nodes.description: Reading, analysis, and interpretation of the Old English poem Beowulf in the original language. Acquaints students with a variety of critical approaches to the poem. A full course description for any given quarter will be available on the English Departments website.

groups: UPPER DIVISION: A-3) Literature or Written Culture (text, writing)

nodes.title: Old English Literature in Translation
groups: UPPER DIVISION: A-3) Literature or Written Culture (text, writing)
nodes.description: Study of Old English prose and verse texts in translation. Considers the history, theory and practice of translating Old English literature. Course contents vary from quarter to quarter: to see what is being taught in any particular quarter, students should consult the course listings on the English Departments website.

groups: UPPER DIVISION: A-3) Literature or Written Culture (text, writing)

nodes.title: Medieval Literature
groups: UPPER DIVISION: A-3) Literature or Written Culture (text, writing)
nodes.prereq_text: Writing 2 or 50 or 109 or English 10; upper-division standing.
nodes.description: Survey of medieval English literature, including such texts as Beowulf, The Canterbury Tales, Morte d'Arthur, Piers Plowman, and Sir Gawain and the Green Knight.

nodes.title: Medieval Literature in Translation
groups: UPPER DIVISION: A-3) Literature or Written Culture (text, writing)
nodes.description: A study of one or more major medieval works in translation such as The Song of Roland, the romances of Chretien de Troyes, the Lais of Marie de France,or The Romance of the Rose.

groups: UPPER DIVISION: A-3) Literature or Written Culture (text, writing)
nodes.prereq_text: Writing 2 or 50 or 109 or English 10 or upper-division standing.
nodes.description: Intensive study of Chaucers poem Troilus and Criseyde, in the original Middle English. Also considers the poems reception history from 1400 to the present through a study of poetic and critical responses. For a full description, consult the course listings on the English Departments website.

groups: UPPER DIVISION: A-3) Literature or Written Culture (text, writing)
nodes.description: An introductory, interdisciplinary approach to the literary and cultural history of France and Francophone world from the Middle Ages and the Renaissance. Readings of poetry, drama, and fiction. Focus on advanced discussion and writing in French.

nodes.title: French Theatre in Translation
groups: UPPER DIVISION: A-3) Literature or Written Culture (text, writing)
nodes.description: A study of French theatre through the centuries, considered within the cultural context of the day (Classicism, the Enlightenment, Romanticism, the Absurd, etc). Plays by Molire, Marivaux, Beaumarchais, Hugo, Musset, Ionesco, and Beckett. Lectures and readings in English.

nodes.title: Voyages to the Unknown
groups: UPPER DIVISION: A-3) Literature or Written Culture (text, writing)
nodes.description: The impact of the voyages of discovery on late 15th- and 16th-century Europe. Readings on real and imaginary voyages: Columbus, Cartier, Lery, More, Rabelais, Montaigne.

nodes.title: World History
nodes.description: Survey of the peoples, cultures, and social, economic, and political systems that have characterized the world's major civilizations in Europe, Asia, Africa, the Americas, and Oceania from prehistory to 1000 CE.

nodes.title: World History
nodes.description: Survey of the peoples, cultures, and social, economic, and political systems that have characterized the world's major civilizations in Europe, Asia, Africa, the Americas, and Oceania from 1000 to 1700 CE.

nodes.title: World History
nodes.description: Survey of the peoples, cultures, and social, economic, and political systems that have characterized the world's major civilizations in Europe, Asia, Africa, the Americas, and Oceania from 1700 to present.

nodes.title: The Ancient Mediterranean and West Asia
nodes.description: Prehistory to 800 CE. History 4A introduces students to the histories of the ancient Mediterranean and West Asia, including Egypt, Greece, Mesopotamia, Persia, and Rome. Lectures and readings examine cultural, economic, intellectual, military, political, religious, and other aspects of the period. Weekly small group sections in which students discuss historical sources and methods are an essential part of this course.

nodes.title: Medieval and Early Modern Europe
nodes.description: Survey of the history of Europe in the Medieval and Early Modern periods, 800-1700. Discusses the major social, political, religious, and cultural characteristics and developments of the period, as well as key interactions between Europe and other parts of the world. Weekly discussion sections are an important feature of this course, enabling students to develop and expand upon material presented during the lecture hour.

nodes.title: Modern Europe
nodes.description: Survey of the history of Modern Europe, 1650-present. Discusses the major social, political, religious, and cultural characteristics and developments of the period, as well as key interactions between Europe and other parts of the world. Weekly discussion sections are an important feature of this course, enabling students to develop and expand upon material presented during the lecture hour.

nodes.title: Historical Investigations: Methods and Skills
nodes.description: Through studying a particular topic in history, students gain insight into historical methods and skills. Course designed for freshmen and sophomore history majors or prospective majors. Others may enroll by permission of instructor. Topics vary by quarter and instructor.

nodes.title: The Middle East from Muhammad to the Nineteenth Century
nodes.description: Introduces students to the history of the Middle East from the rise of Islam until the nineteenth-century Ottoman reforms known as the Tanzimat. Subjects covered include the early caliphates, the influence of Turkic and Mongolian peoples on the region, the Crusades and jihad, the Ottoman and Safavid dynasties, and the interactions between people of different cultural and religious backgrounds in the region.

nodes.title: Survey of African History
nodes.description: Prehistory to c. 1800. History 49-A- B-C is a general survey course designed to introduce students to major themes in African history. The course focuses on organization of production, state formation, African civilizations and identities, science and technology, beliefs and knowledge systems, Africas interaction with the world economy, such as through enslavement and slave trades. Weekly discussion sections are an important feature of this course, enabling students to develop and expand upon material presented during lecture.

nodes.title: Chinese Civilization
nodes.description: A survey of the history of Chinese civilization from 2,000 BCE to the present, focusing on the origins and later development of political, social, economic, philosophical, religious, and cultural traditions.

nodes.title: Japanese History Through Art and Literature
nodes.description: A basic introduction to the history of Japanese culture from its origins to the present day, with particular emphasis on the evidence of architecture and painting (presented through audiovisual modules). Selectedexamples of fiction and poetry will also be used.

groups: UPPER DIVISION: A-4) Religion, Philosophy or Science

nodes.title: The History of Roman Law
nodes.description: Explores Roman law from the archaic 12 Tables through Justinian's 6th century CE Corpus Civilis, analyzing these developments within the broader historical context. Also addresses the influence of Roman law on medieval scholarship and later legal systems.

nodes.title: History of Christianity: Beginning to 800
groups: UPPER DIVISION: A-4) Religion, Philosophy or Science
nodes.prereq_text: History 2A or 4A or Religious Studies 80A or upper-division standing.
nodes.description: The history of Christian communities and doctrines from the first through the eighth centuries. Special emphasis on Christians' evolving relationships with pagan and Jewish communities throughout the Mediterranean world.

nodes.title: The Worlds of Medieval Italy
nodes.prereq_text: History 2B or 4B or upper division standing.
nodes.description: Explores the rich multicultural worlds of medieval Italy, 1000-1300: the Greek south and Muslim Sicily; Norman military conquest and their extraordinary multiethnic aristocratic courts; the commercial revolution and the fluid society of the towns; papal monarchy and religious reactions: saints and heretics; the brutal factional wars of the thirteenth century; popular stories and poetry. The course ends with Dantes Inferno.

nodes.title: The Worlds of Renaissance Italy, 1300-1500
nodes.prereq_text: History 2B or 4B or upper division standing.
nodes.description: Explores the overlapping worlds of Renaissance Italy, 1300-1500: the vibrant merchant culture; the elegant courts of princes; intellectual circles like the Platonic Academy; famed mercenary captains and their troops; the underworld of male same sex relations, of criminality and prostitution; the lives of women in marriages, in convents and in poorhouses; the workshops and homes of the laboring poor. One central theme is the culture of patronage and the production of extraordinary art.

nodes.title: Undergraduate Research Seminar in Medieval European History
nodes.prereq_text: Any one of the following: History 115, 115X, 118A, 118B, 125 or 130 or upper division standing or consent of instructor.

items.text: Any one of the following: HIST 115

nodes.description: Students will conduct historical research in a seminar context, using both primary and secondary source materials. Topics addressed: defining a research problem, identifying an original topic, conducting research, citing sources, and presenting results. Intensive writing required.

nodes.title: Women, The Family, and Sexuality in the Middle Ages
nodes.description: Family structure; perceptions and ideals of intimate and familial relations; status, perceptions, and experiences of women in Western Europe c. 400-1400 A.D. Special attention on social, political, and religious contexts.

nodes.title: Muslims, Christians, and Jews in Medieval Spain: Conquest, Colonization, and Coexistence
nodes.description: Assesses the more than seven centuries of Muslim, Christian, and Jewish coexistence (convivencia) in the Iberian peninsula, examing intercultural and interfaith relations from the time of the Visigoths (fifth century) to the expulsion of the Moriscos (Muslim converts to Christianity) in 1609.

nodes.title: France in the Sixteenth Century
nodes.prereq_text: Hist 2B or 4B or 9 or Upper Division Standing.
nodes.description: Politics, religion, and society and culture in France from the reign of Francois I to Henri IV. Topics include the French Renaissance, religious divisions and civil war, kingship and local authority, family and social hierarchy, and France's relations beyond its borders.

nodes.title: Medieval Medicine: The Discourse and Practices of Medicine in the Middle Ages
groups: UPPER DIVISION: A-4) Religion, Philosophy or Science
nodes.description: Explores medical theory and practice in Western Europe and the Islamic World from the sixth to the sixteenth centuries. Medieval understandings of health, disease and how the body functioned are examined, along with strategies employed to combat injuries and illnesses.

nodes.title: The Middle Ages in Film
nodes.prereq_text: History 4A or 4B or 2B or upper division standing.
nodes.description: Addresses how the Ancient World & the Middle Ages have been portrayed in popular culture & film. Did certain films influence our views of the past and how much we know or think we know about the Ancient World & the Middle Ages? Do these movies influence the way we see the past? We will view films in class & discuss them. Among the topics of these films will be the fall of the Roman Empire, the Crusades and Joan of Arc.

nodes.title: The Middle East I: From the Origins of Islam to the Year 1000
nodes.prereq_text: History 46 or MES 45 or upper-division standing.
nodes.description: The rise of a world religion and the emergence of a new multi-ethnic society under its aegis; the evolution of social and political institutions within the Universal caliphate; the creation of a specifically Islamic culture and intellectual life.

nodes.title: The Middle East II: The Era of Invasions, 1000-1500
nodes.description: The failure of the Caliphate and the search for a new political order; Turkish military and political domination; the structures of urban society; the rebirth of Persian literature; the classical formulations of Islamic religious thought.

nodes.title: Pre-Colonial Southern Africa
nodes.description: Explores the major socio-economic and political history of the Southern African region from around 1000 CE to the 1880s. Focuses on state making, economic systems, regional mobilities and international connections through trade before the advent of European colonialism.

nodes.title: Islam in Africa
nodes.description: Africa is the only continent with a Muslim majority, with more than a quarter of the worlds Muslims living there. Americans tend to associate Islam with Arabs, but Africans greatly outnumber Arabs in the religion. There are more Muslims in Nigeria than in Egypt, more in Ethiopia than Iraq. 1/6th of the worlds Muslims reside in sub-Saharan Africa. How did this come to be? How has the adoption of Islam by Africans shaped their history? And, conversely, how have Africans shaped Islam? We answer these questions by exploring 14 centuries of Islamic African history. We also explore Islam as a system of religious meaning by studying the teachings and writings of African Muslims.

nodes.title: History of Mexico: Pre-Hispanic and Colonial Periods
nodes.description: The history of colonial New Spain, from California to Central America and from the Philippines to the Caribbean. Topics include pre-Columbian societies, including the Aztecs; the formation and development of colonial societies; religion; the economy; and global connections.

nodes.title: History of China
nodes.prereq_text: History 2A or 2B or 2C or 80 or EACS 80 or upper-division standing.
nodes.description: Sixth to seventeenth centuries.

nodes.title: History of Trans-Eurasian Exchanges
nodes.prereq_text: History 2A, or 2B, or 2C, or 4A, or 4B, or 4C, or 80
nodes.description: Eurasia is the largest geographical feature on earth. It gave birth to the earliest civilizations and fostered the antecedents of many modern cultures. Yet, in much historical writing, the regions of Eurasia are treated as isolated units with independent trajectories. This is an artifact of nationalism and ignores the key role that trans-Eurasian interaction played in world history. This course investigates the movement of people, technology, ideas, and images across Eurasia from 3,000 BC to the present. It encourages one to think of a past world without national boundaries, a vast interconnected organism inside which materials and ideas were transmitted in all directions, adapted to the cultural and environmental needs of specific areas.

nodes.title: Japan Under the Tokugawa Shoguns
nodes.prereq_text: History 2A or 2B or 2C or 9 or 87 or upper-division standing.
nodes.description: A survey of Japanese social and cultural history from the mid-sixteenth century to the nineteenth century.

nodes.title: The Samurai
nodes.prereq_text: Hist 9 or 80 or 87 or upper-division standing.
nodes.description: The samurai of Japan were a hereditary military class that evolved over a millennium. Course traces this history and clarifies the range of differences that separated samurai in each era as their roles and ideologies changed.

nodes.title: Dante's Divine Comedy
groups: UPPER DIVISION: A-3) Literature or Written Culture (text, writing)
nodes.description: (Taught in English) Dante's masterpiece, The Divine Comedy, remains among the most astonishing works of world literature. This course follows the pilgram's progress through Inferno, Pergatorio and Paradiso in search of love that moves the sun and the other stars.

nodes.title: Elementary Latin
nodes.description: The beginning course in classical Latin, and first in a three-quarter sequence introducing fundamentals of grammar, syntax, and reading skills. Concepts taught using written exercises. Interesting aspects of Ancient Roman society are introduced.

nodes.title: Elementary Latin
nodes.prereq_text: Latin 1 with a grade of C or better.
nodes.description: A continuation of Latin 1. Emphasis on mastering grammar and building vocabulary.

nodes.title: Intermediate Latin
nodes.prereq_text: Latin 2 with a grade of C or better.
nodes.description: Continuation of Latin 2. Emphasis on building a working vocabulary and the syntax of complex sentences. Reading in classical prose introduce students to ancient Roman literature and culture.

nodes.title: Medieval Latin Readings
groups: UPPER DIVISION: A-3) Literature or Written Culture (text, writing)
nodes.description: Graded and selected reading and study of medieval Latin prose and verse writers.

nodes.title: EMS: Approaches to University Writing for Multilingual Students
nodes.prereq_text: Open to students who have not satisfied the Entry Level Writing Requirement and have a Ling 12 placement or a prerequisite of Ling 3C with a grade of C or better.

requires.text: Open to students who have not satisfied the Entry Level Writing Requirement and have a LING 12 placement or a prerequisite of LING 3C

nodes.description: Principles of critical reading, thinking and writing in the university. Students analyze academic discourse, develop rhetorical strategies for exposition and argument, practice examination writing, and write and revise papers. Completion of C or better meets Entry Level Writing Requirement.

nodes.title: Introduction to Middle East Studies
nodes.description: Surveys the peoples, cultures, and societies of the wider Middle East, focusing on social, political, cultural, and religious change. Among the concepts examined are tradition, modernity, autocracy, religious revival, gender, and ethnicity in their different regional contexts.

nodes.title: History of Philosophy
groups: UPPER DIVISION: A-4) Religion, Philosophy or Science
nodes.description: From Medievals to Rationalists.

nodes.title: Introduction to Buddhism
groups: UPPER DIVISION: A-4) Religion, Philosophy or Science
nodes.description: The historical and cross-cultural exploration of Buddhism through the examination of basic texts, institutions, and practices of diverse Buddhist traditions.

groups: UPPER DIVISION: A-4) Religion, Philosophy or Science

nodes.title: Introduction to Jewish Mysticism
groups: UPPER DIVISION: A-4) Religion, Philosophy or Science
nodes.description: Survey of the major trends of Jewish mysticism from late antiquity through early modernity. Topics include celestial ascent and the angelic transformation of the mystic; letter mysticism and magical techniques; the divine and mystical union; gender and the anthropomorphic representation of God; secrecy and mystical fellowship; ascetic eroticism and the spiritual ideal of worship.

nodes.title: Varieties of Mystical Experience in the Abrahamic Religions: Judaism, Christianity, and Islam
groups: UPPER DIVISION: A-4) Religion, Philosophy or Science
nodes.description: Explores the mystical phenomenon in Judaism, Christianity, and Islam. Topics to be discussed include: language and the limits of reason; the problem of pure consciousness and the contextualization of experience; contemplative vision and the invisible; ascetic renunciation and the eroticism of mystical union; mystical atheism and the antinomian overcoming the law.

groups: UPPER DIVISION: A-4) Religion, Philosophy or Science

nodes.title: Introduction to Daoism
groups: UPPER DIVISION: A-4) Religion, Philosophy or Science
nodes.description: A study of the classical sources of Daoism, followed by a consideration of the varieties of religious practice which developed from those sources.

nodes.title: Nature and Ethics in Chinese Philosophy
groups: UPPER DIVISION: A-4) Religion, Philosophy or Science
nodes.description: A look at how major thinkers in classical Chinese thought grappled with questions related to the individual's place in society and their relationship to their environment. Highlighting their relevance, classical views will be applied to contemporary ethical, social, and environmental debates.

nodes.title: Introduction to Japanese Religion: Texts, Concepts, and Representations
groups: UPPER DIVISION: A-4) Religion, Philosophy or Science
nodes.description: A survey of the main authors, themes, and styles of the Japanese religious and philosophical traditions through readings from and analysis of some significant and influential original texts in English translation.

nodes.title: Religion and Western Civilization I: Ancient
nodes.description: The religions of classical antiquity; myths, rituals, and cults of Greece and Rome; religious dimesions of Greek and Roman philosophy; beginnings anddevelopment of Christianity to time of Theodosius the Great (379-395 C.E.)

nodes.title: Religion and Western Civilization II: Medieval
groups: UPPER DIVISION: A-4) Religion, Philosophy or Science
nodes.description: The decline of classical antiquity; the emergence of medieval Christendom; religion and culture of the Middle Ages (eleventh-thirteenth centuries); subsequent development of the Renaissance and Reformation.

nodes.title: The New Testament and Early Christianity
groups: UPPER DIVISION: A-4) Religion, Philosophy or Science
nodes.description: Study of the varieties of early Christian traditions and literature of the first century, with special (but not exclusive) attention to the new testament.

nodes.title: Second-Century Christianity
groups: UPPER DIVISION: A-4) Religion, Philosophy or Science
nodes.description: Study of the various religious trends in developing Christianity as represented in the writings of the early Fathers, the later books of the New Testament, the New Testament Apocrypha, and "heretical" movements.

nodes.title: Introduction to Islamic Law
groups: UPPER DIVISION: A-4) Religion, Philosophy or Science
nodes.description: Addresses the Islamic legal concepts of rights and responsibilities and the relationship between the individual and the state in Islamic law. The course also provides an overview of the history and development of Islamic law and legal theories.

nodes.title: The Qur'an and Its Interpretations
groups: UPPER DIVISION: A-4) Religion, Philosophy or Science
nodes.description: Introduces the Qur'an from different perspectives: A source of spiritual guidance, a political document, a source of law and philosophy, an inspiration for visual and acoustic arts, and a piece of literature of interest to literary criticism.

groups: UPPER DIVISION: A-4) Religion, Philosophy or Science

nodes.title: Christian Thought and Cultures of the Ancient World
groups: UPPER DIVISION: A-4) Religion, Philosophy or Science
nodes.description: Outline of the primary philosophical, sociological, and cultural trends in the first four centuries of Christianity: The changing relationship to imperial government, the "parting of the ways" with Judaism, the cultural inheritance of paganism, problems of self-definition against heresies.

nodes.title: Christian Thought and Cultures of the Middle Ages
groups: UPPER DIVISION: A-4) Religion, Philosophy or Science
nodes.description: Exploration of some of the major intellectual and cultural developments defining medieval Christian Europe. Materials considered include both contemporary historical studies and selected primary sources in theology, philosophy, literature, and the arts.

nodes.title: Introduction to Rabbinic Literature
groups: UPPER DIVISION: A-4) Religion, Philosophy or Science
nodes.description: An introduction to the basic texts of Rabbinic literature through an analysis of representative passages from the Mishnah, Talmud, and Midrash. Particular attention will be given to the various types of Midrash and the principles and methods of Midrashic interpretation. (Knowledge of Hebrew not required.)

nodes.title: Holy Delight: Eros and the Sacred in Jewish and Christian Interpretations of the Song of Songs
groups: UPPER DIVISION: A-4) Religion, Philosophy or Science
nodes.description: Explores the allegorical and symbolic interpretations of the biblical love poem known as the Song of Songs in the Jewish and Christian traditions from Late Antiquity to the Middle Ages. Topics to be discussed include the Song in its literary and historical context, the interplay of the sacred and the erotic in religious experience, allegory and the sacralization of the erotic, Marian interpretations and the ascetic curbing of desire, and the contemplative and ectastic interpretations of medieval kabbalists.

groups: UPPER DIVISION: A-4) Religion, Philosophy or Science
UPPER DIVISION: A-4) Religion, Philosophy or Science
UPPER DIVISION: A-4) Religion, Philosophy or Science

nodes.title: Islamic Traditions
groups: UPPER DIVISION: A-4) Religion, Philosophy or Science
nodes.description: Introduction to history, doctrines, and practices of the Sunni, Shi'i and Sufi expressions of Islam. Includes study of Qur'an, Hadith literature, religious law, leadership, and holy places.

nodes.title: The Problem of Evil in Religious Traditions
groups: UPPER DIVISION: A-3) Literature or Written Culture (text, writing)
nodes.description: This course surveys key philosophical formulations and responses to the problem of evil, including natural evil (e.g. diseases) and moral evil (e.g. injustices), as expressed across religious traditions, including the Ancient Greeks, Judaism, Christianity and Islam. The focus of the course is a comparative reading of philosophical and religious primary sources in their historical and cultural contexts.

groups: UPPER DIVISION: A-4) Religion, Philosophy or Science
UPPER DIVISION: A-4) Religion, Philosophy or Science

nodes.title: Islamic Humanism
nodes.description: Investigates humanist themes that were the product of the Arab-Islamic reception of Greek thought in the early and classical period of Islamic history (~800- 1258) as championed in the works of literators, philosophers, and historians. The objective of this course is to introduce these humanist themes through close reading and examination of primary sources in their historical, multicultural, and multi-religious contexts.

nodes.title: Islamic Philosophy and Theology
groups: UPPER DIVISION: A-4) Religion, Philosophy or Science
nodes.description: This course surveys the history of rationalist thought in pre-modern Islamic history, focusing on the genesis and development of the disciplines of rationalist theology and Neoplatonized Aristotelian philosophy. The objective of this course is to highlight the experimental and dynamic scope of rationalist thought in pre-modern Islamic history through close reading of primary sources in their broader historical and intellectual contexts.

groups: UPPER DIVISION: A-4) Religion, Philosophy or Science

nodes.title: Religion in Japanese Culture
groups: UPPER DIVISION: A-4) Religion, Philosophy or Science
nodes.description: A historical analysis of the major components of the classical and medieval religious systems of Japan, through investigation of texts, rituals, and institutions.

nodes.title: Elementary Spanish I
nodes.description: Students will learn to use Spanish for communication in real, meaningful situations. This course will develop an understanding of basic grammatical concepts along with obtaining an appreciation of the various cultures of the Spanish-speaking world. The course follows a communicative approach and class time is primarily used for communication practice and Spanish will be spoken in class 99% of the time. By the end of this course students are expected to develop proficiency at the Novice-mid level.

nodes.title: Hybrid Elementary Spanish I
nodes.description: SPAN 1HY is the first course in a three-part hybrid Spanish series (SPAN 1HY, 2HY, 3HY), equivalent to the SPAN 1, 2, 3 Elementary Spanish sequence. Combining face-to-face instruction with online work, this course uses a communicative approach to develop basic Spanish skills for real-life situations. Class time focuses on active communication, with 99% of instruction conducted in Spanish. Students will build foundational grammar skills and gain insight into the diverse cultures of the Spanish-speaking world. By the end of the course, students are expected to reach Novice-Mid proficiency.

nodes.title: Elementary Spanish II
nodes.prereq_text: Spanish 1 or Spanish W1 with a grade of P or a grade of C or higher.
nodes.description: Students will learn to use Spanish for communication in real, meaningful situations. This course will develop an understanding of basic grammatical concepts along with obtaining an appreciation of the various cultures of the Spanish-speaking world. The course follows a communicative approach and class time is primarily used for communication practice and Spanish will be spoken in class 99% of the time. By the end of this course students are expected to develop proficiency at the Novice-high level.

nodes.title: Hybrid Elementary Spanish II
nodes.prereq_text: Spanish 1 or Spanish 1HY with a grade of P or a grade of C or higher.
nodes.description: SPAN 2HY is the second of the three Hybrid Elementary Spanish courses. Its hybrid format combines increased individual work with the online textbook, materials, and other web-based activities with reduced face-to-face class time and live guided conversation sessions. Course materials and activities focus on consolidating the same array of skills promoted in SPAN 2. Students learn to use Spanish for communication in real, meaningful situations, develop an understanding of basic grammatical concepts and an appreciation of the various cultures of the Spanish-speaking world.

nodes.title: Elementary Spanish III
nodes.prereq_text: Spanish 2 or Spanish W2 with a grade of P or a grade of C or higher.
nodes.description: Students will learn to use Spanish for communication in real, meaningful situations. This course will develop an understanding of basic grammatical concepts along with obtaining an appreciation of various cultures of the Spanish-speaking world. The course follows a communicative approach and class time is primarily used for communication practice; Spanish will be spoken in class 99% of the time. By the end of this course students are expected to develop proficiency at the Novice-high or Intermediate-low level.

nodes.title: Hybrid Elementary Spanish III
nodes.prereq_text: Completion of Spanish 2 or Spanish 2HY with a grade of P, or a grade of C or higher.
nodes.description: SPAN 3HY is the third of the three Hybrid Elementary Spanish courses. Its hybrid format combines increased individual work with the online textbook, materials, and other web-based activities with reduced face-to-face class time and live guided conversation sessions. Course materials and activities focus on consolidating the same array of skills promoted in SPAN 3. Students learn to use Spanish for communication in real, meaningful situations, develop an understanding of basic grammatical concepts and an appreciation of the various cultures of the Spanish-speaking world.

nodes.title: Intermediate Spanish I
nodes.prereq_text: Spanish 3, Spanish 3SS, 3HY, with a grade of P or a grade of C or higher; or a score of 3 on the AP Spanish Language Examination; or a score of 3 on the AP Spanish Language & Culture Examination.
nodes.description: Begins review of basic grammar and syntax.

nodes.title: Intermediate Spanish II
nodes.prereq_text: Spanish 4 with a grade of P or a grade of C or higher; or a score of 4 on the AP Spanish Language Examination; or a score of 4 on the AP Spanish Language and Culture Examination; or a score of 3 on the AP Spanish Literature and Culture Examination.
nodes.description: Continues the review of basic grammar and syntax. Course conducted in Spanish.

nodes.title: Intermediate Spanish III
nodes.prereq_text: Spanish 5 with a grade of P or a grade of C or higher; or a score of 5 on the AP Spanish Language Examination; or a score of 5 on the AP Spanish Language and Culture Examination; or a score of 3 on the AP Spanish Literature Examination; or a score of 4 on the AP Spanish Literature and Culture Examination.
nodes.description: An intensive course designed to develop students' skills in reading, oral, and written expression by reading and discussing Hispanic texts, and writing compositions on related topics.

nodes.title: Intermediate Spanish for Heritage Speakers
nodes.prereq_text: Instructor or department approval required to finalize enrollment.
nodes.description: SPAN 15 is designed for students who learned Spanish at home or as a first language and provides them with the language and learning skills required to successfully complete more advanced Spanish courses (SPAN 16A/B). It focuses on formal Spanish, grammar, and reading with an emphasis on writing and vocabulary building. Students will develop awareness of linguistic registers, and practice formal speaking and writing skills through readings and discussions based on Hispanic topics in the United States and other Spanish-speaking countries. Special attention will be paid to those aspects that Spanish speakers in the United States find most problematic.

nodes.title: Spanish for Heritage Speakers
nodes.description: Addresses on a university level the needs and strengths of students with Spanish speaking background but no formal language training in Spanish speaking countries. Emphasizes skill in composition, advanced reading comprehension, standard versus vernacular usages, cross language interference, etc.

nodes.title: Spanish for Heritage Speakers
nodes.prereq_text: Spanish 16A with a grade of P or a grade of C or higher.
nodes.description: Addresses on university level the needs and strengths of students with Spanish speaking background but no formal language training in Spanish speaking countries. Emphasizes more complex skills in composition and advanced reading comprehension than Spanish 16A, as well as standard versus vernacular usages, cross language interferences, etc.

nodes.title: Advanced Grammar and Composition
nodes.prereq_text: Spanish 6 with a grade of P or a grade of C or higher; or a score of 4 or 5 on the AP Spanish Literature Examination; or a score of 5 on the AP Spanish Literature and Culture Examination.
nodes.description: Intensive course taught in Spanish designed to reinforce students' comprehension and ability to express themselves in Spanish, both orally and in writing, and to develop the students' vocabularies and awareness of syntactical structures in the language.

nodes.title: Spanish Literature from the Beginning to the Present
groups: UPPER DIVISION: A-3) Literature or Written Culture (text, writing)
nodes.description: Medieval Spanish literature.

nodes.title: Non-Castilian Literatures of Spain
groups: UPPER DIVISION: A-3) Literature or Written Culture (text, writing)
nodes.description: Introduction to Spains medieval linguistic and cultural diversity through literary works written in such languages as Latin, Arabic, Hebrew, Mozarabic, Occitan, Catalan-Valencian, Galician-Portuguese and Galician. Texts read in Spanish or English translation.

groups: UPPER DIVISION: A-3) Literature or Written Culture (text, writing)
UPPER DIVISION: A-3) Literature or Written Culture (text, writing)

nodes.title: Online Elementary Spanish I
nodes.description: Span W1 is the first course of the Elementary Spanish three course sequence delivered in a fully online format. By the end of this course students are expected to develop basic proficiency in Spanish at the Novice-mid level.

nodes.title: Online Elementary Spanish II
nodes.prereq_text: Spanish 1 with a grade of P or a grade of C or higher.
nodes.description: SPAN W 2 is the second of the three Elementary Spanish courses offered in a fully online format. Its online format combines technology-based language instruction with online class meetings and live guided conversation sessions. Course materials and activities focus on consolidating the same array of skills promoted in the regular Elementary Span II course. Students learn to use Spanish for communication in real, meaningful situations, develop an understanding of basic grammatical concepts and an appreciation of the various cultures of the Spanish-speaking world. Each week, students attend one online class session and one conversation session. There is individual work with the textbook, online materials, and other web-based activities.

nodes.title: Academic Writing
nodes.prereq_text: Satisfaction of the Entry Level Writing requirement or Linguistics 12 with a grade of "C" or better.

items.text: Satisfaction of the Entry Level Writing requirement

nodes.description: A writing course focusing on developing analytical skills, synthesizing multiple sources, sustaining coherent arguments, and revising for clarity of style. Reading and writing assignments are drawn from a range of academic disciplines.

nodes.title: Academic Writing for Engineers
nodes.prereq_text: Satisfaction of the Entry Level Writing requirement or Linguistics 12; freshmen only; open to ECE, Chemical Engineering, Mechanical Engineering, and Computer Engineering majors only.

items.text: Satisfaction of the Entry Level Writing requirement
open to ECE, Chemical Engineering, Mechanical Engineering, and Computer Engineering majors only

nodes.description: A writing course focusing on developing analytical skills, synthesizing multiple sources, sustaining coherent arguments, and revising for clarity of style. Reading and writing assignments are drawn from a range of engineering disciplines.

nodes.title: Writing and the Research Process
nodes.description: A writing course addressing the analytical skills underlying the research processes of various academic and professional communities. Sections vary in topic and disciplinary emphasis.

nodes.title: Writing for the Disciplines
nodes.description: Analysis and practice of various forms of academic and professional writing for and in the disciplines.
